query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Degradation during elevated-temperature exposure is governed by the selective oxidation of reactive elements—primarily Cr and Ti—which form continuous, brittle oxide scales that build up high internal tensile stresses. Once the oxide scale exceeds a critical thickness, interfacial decohesion and spallation set in, creating crack nucleation sites that rapidly lead to catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a supersaturated FCC matrix and fine microstructural features.
generation.intervention: Perform controlled exposure tests comparing different oxygen partial pressures in the gas atmosphere to isolate oxidation effects.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures above approximately 900 K under oxidizing conditions (e.g., 10 mbar O2) versus inert atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and propagation of continuous, brittle oxide scales—primarily Cr-rich and Ti-rich—along grain boundaries and surface layers.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, reactive elements preferentially oxidize. As the oxide layer grows beyond a critical thickness (e.g., >20–30 nm), internal stresses accumulate until the interface can no longer remain coherent, leading to spallation. This spallation acts as a locus for rapid crack initiation and catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples tested in an oxidizing environment will show significantly thicker oxide scales, measurable mass loss from spallation, and reduced tensile ductility relative to samples tested in inert conditions.
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured alloy tested under inert atmospheres at the same elevated temperatures with minimal oxide formation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism dominates when oxidation induces oxide scales thicker than the critical limit (approximately 20–30 nm) at temperatures above ~900 K.
generation.uncertainty: Exact numerical thresholds for oxide thickness and the precise internal stress levels required to trigger spallation need further calibration; meanwhile, minor contributions from oxidation of Mn and Al are assumed secondary.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose identical alloy samples to a controlled oxidizing atmosphere (with a specified oxygen partial pressure) and to an inert atmosphere at temperatures above ~900 K. Post-exposure, characterize the oxide scale formation using TEM/SEM and assess mechanical properties via tensile tests.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and continuity (by TEM/SEM)
Mass loss attributable to oxide spallation
Tensile ductility, strength, and fracture mode analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant differences in oxide scale development, spallation mass loss, or mechanical degradation are observed between oxidizing and inert conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Cr’s outward diffusion is faster than oxygen’s inward diffusion, so chromia scales usually grow outward, consisting of fractions of iron, nickel, and manganese. However, at temperatures above 900 °C, chromia can form volatile CrO3. Aluminum, another effective alloying element, forms a protective Al2O3 layer, offering significant resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion. Al2O3 scales grow slower than chromium oxide scales and are more stable, especially against aggressive carbon or sulfur species. However, the formation of alumina and consequent depletion of Al in the alloy could result in structural instability in the alloy. The formation of oxide scales in HEAs containing multiple oxide-forming species is influenced by their intricate chemistries and microstructures. High-temperature, long-duration oxidation studies on bulk alloys typically reveal dominant oxide films composed of complex ternary and quaternary oxides. The polycrystalline nature of these alloys, combined with surface heterogeneity and phase instabilities at high temperatures, leads to highly variable oxide structures. cited_evidence.text: Although it was not reported in the literature that this alloy would form second phase precipitates, our experimental and computational results show that such precipitation occurs. At these levels, this precipitation could be beneficial to nuclear applications. Indeed, second phase precipitates may increase the high-temperature strength of the alloy. This is important since presently, the only alloy with demonstrable data as structural material for MSRs is Hastelloy-N, but it does not have sufficient creep strength. In addition, precipitate/matrix interfaces can act as irradiation induced point defect sinks, increasing the alloy’s resistance to irradiation damage. Finally, since Cr is immobilized as precipitates in the surface regions beneath the alloy/salt interface, it could not potentially dissolve in the salt and would still be available at levels sufficient to prevent air oxidation on the outer side of the piping. Thus, both the molten salt (depletion of Mn) and ageing (Cr rich precipitate) are effects occurring in-operando which could improve the resistance of this HEA to degradation in MSR environment.
